lines.text: Good morning. I'm Amara Nwosu, gastroenterology and hepatology. Nine metres of tube, and what goes on in it.
We'll follow a meal: acid in the stomach, the hormones that coordinate everything, digestion and absorption, and then the liver, bile and bilirubin.

slide.heading: Stomach acid
bullets: Parietal cells: H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the proton pump)
Stimulated by gastrin, histamine (H2) and ACh
PPIs block the pump irreversibly
Parietal cells also make intrinsic factor
B12 + intrinsic factor absorbed in the terminal ileum

lines.text: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid through the H-K ATPase, the proton pump.
Three signals switch them on: gastrin, histamine through H2 receptors, and acetylcholine from the vagus.
Proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole bind the pump irreversibly. They're the strongest acid suppressants we have.
Parietal cells make one more thing: intrinsic factor, which carries vitamin B12 to the end of the ileum to be absorbed.

slide.heading: The hormones that run digestion
bullets: Gastrin (G cells, antrum): acid
CCK (I cells, duodenum): gallbladder, enzymes
Secretin (S cells, duodenum): bicarbonate
CCK responds to fat and protein; secretin to acid

lines.text: Food reaching the duodenum sets off hormones from its lining.
Fat and protein release cholecystokinin, which contracts the gallbladder and releases pancreatic enzymes. That's why a fatty meal brings on gallstone pain.
Acid releases secretin, which calls for bicarbonate from the pancreas to neutralize it.

slide.heading: Breaking it down and taking it in
bullets: Starch: amylase, then brush-border enzymes
Lactase deficiency: osmotic diarrhea, bloating
Proteins: pepsin, then trypsin (activated by enteropeptidase)
Fats: bile salts make micelles; chylomicrons to lymph
Bile salts reabsorbed in the terminal ileum

lines.text: Starch is broken down by amylase and finished by enzymes on the brush border of the small intestine, including lactase.
Many adults lose their lactase. Unabsorbed lactose draws water into the gut and bacteria ferment it: bloating, gas and diarrhea.
Fats need bile. Bile salts emulsify them into micelles; enterocytes package them into chylomicrons, which go into the lymph. Then the bile salts are reabsorbed at the end of the ileum and recycled.

slide.heading: Bilirubin: follow the yellow
bullets: Heme → unconjugated bilirubin (insoluble, on albumin)
Liver conjugates it (UGT1A1)
Hemolysis: unconjugated rises
Obstruction: conjugated rises; dark urine, pale stool
Gilbert syndrome: mild unconjugated rise with fasting

lines.text: Old red cells release heme, which becomes unconjugated bilirubin. It's insoluble, so it travels on albumin.

The liver conjugates it with glucuronic acid, making it water-soluble, and excretes it in bile. Gut bacteria turn it into urobilinogen: some colors the stool brown, some is reabsorbed and leaves in the urine.
Too much production, as in hemolysis, raises unconjugated bilirubin. A blocked bile duct backs up conjugated bilirubin into the blood.
And a benign, common variant: Gilbert syndrome, a sluggish UGT enzyme. Mild jaundice when fasting or ill, nothing else.

slide.heading: Acetaminophen overdose
bullets: Normally glucuronidated and sulfated
In overdose, more goes to NAPQI (via CYP2E1)
Glutathione detoxifies NAPQI until it runs out
Then centrilobular hepatic necrosis
N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione: give it early

lines.text: The most common cause of acute liver failure in the United States is acetaminophen.
At normal doses it's conjugated and excreted. In overdose, more is turned into a toxic metabolite, NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes until the glutathione runs out. Then liver cells die.
